html:
The tradition of thought that grew from the teachings of Confucius (551 to 479 BCE), which shaped government, family life and learning in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for two thousand years.

Its core is that a good society rests on good people in proper relationships: ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger, friend and friend. Its key ideas are humaneness (ren), ritual and manners (li), and respect for parents (filial piety). Rulers should govern by moral example more than by punishment, and officials should be chosen for learning and virtue, not birth. Mencius taught that human nature is good; Xunzi that it must be shaped by training.

Under the Han dynasty it became the official learning of the state, though in practice it mixed with the harder methods of the Legalists. The Discourses on Salt and Iron of 81 BCE record Confucian scholars arguing against state monopolies. Later the imperial examinations tested candidates on the Confucian classics. From the 1100s Zhu Xi remade the tradition as Neo-Confucianism, and his readings became the exam standard until 1905.

It spread with Chinese writing. Prince Shōtoku's Seventeen-article Constitution in Japan draws on it, Vietnam's Hồng Đức Code follows it, and Joseon Korea made it the state creed. In the 1900s reformers blamed it for backwardness: the May Fourth Movement of 1919 attacked it in China, as Fukuzawa Yukichi had in Japan.
sum: The tradition of thought that grew from the teachings of Confucius (551 to 479 BCE), which shaped government, family life and learning in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for two thousand years.
